card.title: ZCG and the dev fund
card.byline: Zcash forum threads on whether to end, shrink, restructure or redirect the Zcash Community Grants stream and treasury, and how Zcash development should be funded.

output.headline: What should happen to Zcash’s grants funding?

overview.text: Zcash Community Grants (ZCG) pays for development and adoption projects; these threads debate whether to stop, shrink or redirect its funding and existing savings.
Participants disagree about who should control the money, whether grants deliver enough value, and whether private funding could replace them.
The October 2026 snapshot contains competing proposals, including reserves for future mining rewards, but leaves the amounts, safeguards and decision process contested.

points.text: Critics allege self-dealing: coinholders bear dilution but a foundation-selected community panel elects ZCG. The opening proposal says 36% of panel members received grants and argues that funders lack control while recipients have influence.

Critics question grant outcomes and adult-industry spending. They cite another $455K for Zcash Shielded Assets (ZSAs) after a 98.6% opposing poll result, interpreting it as disregard for holders. The poll’s scope and representativeness are disputed.

Stream opponents argue that a treasury reported above $100M exceeds a committee designed for under $10M, regardless of past performance. They say continued inflows add millions weekly and allege that ZCG delayed proposing its own response.

Committee critics argue that users and builders know needs better than five allocators. They expect donors, companies and crowdfunding, as in Bitcoin or Linux, to fill funding gaps; holders can fund favored projects directly.

Defenders say the ZSA poll was advisory, concerned protocol inclusion, and measured participating coin weight rather than all holders. They describe the later grant as preserving and integrating prior work, while its additional value remains challenged.

Grant defenders argue that development and adoption work remain unfinished. They want experienced leadership and long-term budgets, and doubt private funding will reliably support research, community work or new teams without investor connections.

Critics of coinholder control warn of low turnout, anonymous wealth-weighted votes and capture. They argue that the protocol’s independent grants allocation matters: bearing dilution costs does not by itself establish exclusive authority over ZCG.

Supporters cite wallet hosting, Ledger and Trezor support, Arti, payments, bridges and security work as ZCG successes. They point to rejected proposals and few failures among hundreds of grants; critics dispute what the track record demonstrates.

Reformers propose restructuring rather than dissolving ZCG: clearer goals, specialized grant tracks, accountable program managers, experienced leadership or a legal trust. These alternatives change oversight without necessarily ending grants.

Some participants want both ZCG and coinholder funding streams ended, or both left until the planned 2028 expiry. They argue that cutting only ZCG concentrates power; some also believe the fund has served its purpose and private capital can replace it.

Others want separate decisions for ZCG and coinholder grants, citing direct votes on individual coinholder awards and security or infrastructure work they value. They distinguish stopping future inflows from reallocating the existing treasury.

Reserve advocates say the Network Sustainability Mechanism (NSM) holds funds out of circulation and later pays miners over decades without a grant committee. They stress that this reserve exists independently of proposals to end ZCG’s stream.

Opponents say redirecting funds to the NSM shifts resources from development to miners, with payouts described as starting around 2031 and a second issuance curve. Some allege mining interests motivate the change; those motive claims are not established.

Compromise supporters favor ending or tapering inflows, donating part of the treasury to the NSM and retaining grants capacity. The Financial Privacy Foundation reports counsel’s view that donation is lawful with an affirmative community vote and accepted proposal.

Compromise critics say tapering to 2032 leaves accountability unresolved. They question the proposed 55% donation, its sensitivity to ZEC’s price, the absence of a dollar cap, and who a future legal-defense fund would protect or how quickly it could act.

Opponents of rushing or reallocating holdings argue there is no emergency and existing funds have a restricted community purpose. Some accept stopping inflows but want treasuries retained, months of consultation, better polling and clarity about authority.

Zcash Adoption Pool (ZAP) supporters see grants for people who need private payments as the existing mandate: debanked people, sex workers, refugees and small businesses. They favor targeted outreach and ongoing use; the draft guarantees no recipient a grant.

ZAP critics question lasting use after recipients cash out, citing airdrop retention figures and demanding metrics. They also oppose shared issuance funding contested social causes; some favor voluntary giving. Supporters dispute the airdrop comparison.

Participants condemn reported transphobic and antisemitic attacks around the ZECsy outreach grant. They argue that at-risk groups, including sex workers, legitimately need private payments and that disagreement over spending does not excuse identity attacks.

Spending critics distinguish access to Zcash from subsidies for particular campaigns or causes. They argue that objections to public funding, including adult-industry events, should be answered on their merits rather than treated as attacks on identity.

description.text: The disagreement is over whether accountability comes from coinholder control, an independent committee, or a different balance of power.

decision_at_stake.text: Who should decide which projects receive grants?

positions_with_post_references.label: Coinholder control
positions_with_post_references.text: Critics say holders bear the cost of new issuance but cannot directly choose ZCG’s committee, creating conflicts between funders and recipients.

positions_with_post_references.label: Independent community funding
positions_with_post_references.text: Others warn that anonymous, wealth-weighted votes can concentrate power too; they defend a community channel independent of large holders.

unresolved_status.text: The posts do not establish which arrangement would best represent those affected or constrain capture in practice.

shared_premises_if_actually_shared.text: Both the opening proposal and its detailed rebuttal recognize holders’ economic exposure to issuance; they disagree about what authority follows.

disputed_factual_claims.text: The opening proposal cites grant-recipient participation in the panel as evidence of conflicts. Critics of coin voting cite particular awards and anonymous wealth concentration. Neither set of examples alone measures comparative capture risk.

disputed_values_or_authority.text: Does bearing dilution costs confer exclusive spending authority, or should the protocol preserve independent community and coinholder roles?

evidence_and_its_limits.text: Panel membership figures and examples of controversial votes are arguments offered in the posts, not an independently verified audit of either governance system.

strongest_material_objections.text: Replacing a committee with coin-weighted voting can shift concentration rather than remove it. Defending independence alone also does not answer scrutiny of committee conflicts.

what_would_resolve_or_clarify.text: Compare conflict rules, voter concentration, proposal scrutiny and appeal mechanisms under each option; separate the current mandate from the mandate people want.

description.text: Critics see poor outcomes and ignored preferences; supporters cite useful infrastructure and dispute what a prominent poll required.

decision_at_stake.text: Does ZCG’s record justify keeping a grants program?

positions_with_post_references.label: Question the spending
positions_with_post_references.text: Critics point to disputed grants and further Zcash Shielded Assets (ZSA) funding after a strongly negative coin-weighted poll.

positions_with_post_references.label: Count the benefits
positions_with_post_references.text: Supporters cite wallets and security work. They say the ZSA poll was advisory and further spending maintained earlier work, though its added value still needs justification.

unresolved_status.text: Participants still disagree about value for money and what the poll should have changed.

disputed_factual_claims.text: The cited 98.6% is challenged as a share of participating coin weight, not a count of all holders. Defenders also distinguish sentiment about protocol inclusion from an instruction to halt all ZSA work.

disputed_values_or_authority.text: Participants differ on how strongly an advisory poll should constrain an independent grant committee and which outcomes count as worthwhile.

evidence_and_its_limits.text: A supporter lists funded infrastructure and links a grants spreadsheet. That is evidence offered for a track record, not by itself a cost-effectiveness comparison or proof of adoption.

strongest_material_objections.text: Past spending alone cannot justify the next grant, but leaving code available is not the same as maintaining compatibility or completing integration. The additional work needs its own case.

what_would_resolve_or_clarify.text: Compare cost, delivered work and measurable benefit grant by grant, and state what action each poll was intended to authorize.

description.text: An enlarged treasury prompts calls to stop or taper inflows, while others see unfinished work and unreliable private alternatives.

decision_at_stake.text: Should future funding stop, shrink, or continue?

positions_with_post_references.label: Stop the inflows
positions_with_post_references.text: Some say the treasury is already too large and private funding can replace grants; others want both grants streams treated alike.

positions_with_post_references.label: Taper or keep funding
positions_with_post_references.text: ZCG proposes a taper. Defenders of continued funding see unfinished work and doubt private investors will reliably support it.

positions_with_post_references.label: Decide separately
positions_with_post_references.text: Another position separates future inflows from existing holdings and treats the two grants mechanisms as different choices.

unresolved_status.text: A budget and replacement-funding case remain contested.

shared_premises_if_actually_shared.text: ZCG’s own taper announcement and stream opponents agree that present inflows exceed its spending capacity; they propose different responses.

disputed_factual_claims.text: One proposal says private funding is no longer scarce. A reply disputes that premise, distinguishing plentiful public funds from a small pool of private investors.

disputed_values_or_authority.text: Some oppose leaving only the coinholder stream because it concentrates power. Others want each mechanism judged separately rather than made conditional on the other.

evidence_and_its_limits.text: Treasury valuations and runway estimates depend on ZEC’s price and spending assumptions. A fixed coin amount does not by itself establish a dollar budget or a reliable funding horizon.

strongest_material_objections.text: A large treasury need not imply that useful work is finished; conversely, useful past work does not settle whether further inflows are needed.

what_would_resolve_or_clarify.text: Compare annual needs, price scenarios and replacement funding for both streams, distinguishing a pause in new receipts from changes to existing savings.

description.text: Proposals divide money between grants, future mining rewards and development reserves; even compromise supporters question the amounts and safeguards.

decision_at_stake.text: What should happen to redirected funding and existing savings?

positions_with_post_references.label: Reserve for mining rewards
positions_with_post_references.text: Supporters favor the Network Sustainability Mechanism (NSM), a reserve for future miner payments without a grant committee.

positions_with_post_references.label: Keep grants capacity
positions_with_post_references.text: Alternatives restructure ZCG, retain its savings, or combine a partial donation with reserves for development and legal defense.

positions_with_post_references.label: Scrutinize the compromise
positions_with_post_references.text: Critics question the donation percentage, price exposure, missing dollar cap and future access to legal support.

unresolved_status.text: Neither the allocation nor its safeguards are settled in these posts.

disputed_factual_claims.text: Critics allege mining interests benefit from redirecting grants. The opening proposal discloses a mining connection but says the initiative is personal; a financial connection does not establish the alleged motive.

disputed_values_or_authority.text: Preserving grants capacity and reserving future miner rewards serve different priorities. Others object to moving existing holdings even if new inflows stop.

evidence_and_its_limits.text: ZCG’s taper presents future reserve and reward projections. A reply separates projected coin subsidies from dollar revenues or actual security; these projections are not measured future outcomes.

strongest_material_objections.text: A midpoint donation is not a derived budget. Critics also ask whether the legal reserve could assist an unpopular contributor promptly; the posts do not answer that operational question.

what_would_resolve_or_clarify.text: Specify the intended runway, price assumptions, spending authority and legal-support eligibility, then derive allocations from those goals rather than a midpoint.

description.text: The debate combines lasting use, limits on shared funding, and the distinction between criticizing grants and attacking recipients’ identities.

decision_at_stake.text: What should adoption funding pay for?

positions_with_post_references.label: Reach people who need privacy
positions_with_post_references.text: Zcash Adoption Pool (ZAP) supporters favor targeted outreach to people needing private payments, distinguishing it from indiscriminate airdrops.

positions_with_post_references.label: Show lasting benefit
positions_with_post_references.text: Critics question retention and shared funding for contested causes; some prefer voluntary donations and require metrics before spending.

positions_with_post_references.label: Separate spending from identity
positions_with_post_references.text: Participants condemn reported identity attacks; others insist that objections to grant spending still deserve answers on their merits.

unresolved_status.text: The posts leave both adoption standards and funding boundaries contested.

disputed_factual_claims.text: One critic cites airdrop figures of 5–25% continued activity; a reply argues that targeted outreach reaches different users with different needs. Whether those figures predict ZAP outcomes is disputed.

disputed_values_or_authority.text: The disagreement includes whether shared issuance should fund particular causes at all, not just whether recipients use ZEC. The draft presents broad adoption as the existing mandate; critics prefer direct holder benefit or opt-in giving.

evidence_and_its_limits.text: The linked airdrop study is evidence cited by a participant, not an independently verified evaluation of this proposal. The ZAP draft still requires grant assessment and does not award funds to listed groups automatically.

strongest_material_objections.text: Funding a recipient need not establish ongoing currency use; targeted outreach need not behave like an airdrop. Spending criticism and condemnation of identity attacks can coexist without resolving the grant’s merits.

what_would_resolve_or_clarify.text: Define retention and real-use measures for a bounded outreach pilot, alongside explicit grant eligibility. Evaluate spending evidence separately from claims about recipients’ identities.

issues.issue: How should a change be decided?

description.text: Calls for timely action meet objections about consultation, polling and authority to redirect funds already held.

decision_at_stake.text: What process should authorize changes to inflows and existing funds?

positions_with_post_references.label: Act while funds accumulate
positions_with_post_references.text: Stream opponents say delay adds millions and ZCG already had time to propose a response; some compromise supporters urge consolidation.

positions_with_post_references.label: Consult and clarify authority
positions_with_post_references.text: Others want months of discussion and resist moving existing holdings. The Financial Privacy Foundation reports counsel permits a donation after a community vote and accepted proposal.

unresolved_status.text: Claims about urgency, consent and adequate representation remain in conflict.

disputed_factual_claims.text: One account says ZCG delayed a promised proposal after a month of discussion. Another says the debate arrived as a fabricated emergency and requires months more. These accounts are presented as participants’ claims, not a verified procedural history.

disputed_values_or_authority.text: Opponents characterize reallocating existing holdings as taking restricted community funds without sufficient authority. The Financial Privacy Foundation reports a conditional legal route; that report does not establish community consent.

evidence_and_its_limits.text: The supplied post reports counsel’s conclusion, not the underlying opinion. Statements that a compromise has the most support are participants’ judgments, not a demonstrated consensus.

strongest_material_objections.text: Stopping future inflows and donating existing holdings are separate decisions. Support for one does not establish authorization for the other.

what_would_resolve_or_clarify.text: Publish separate decisions, voting scope, authority requirements and a consultation timetable, including how holders and other affected participants will be represented.
